sewage-treatment-s1.title: Wastewater quality through a treatment plant

table.caption: Average wastewater measurements at each point in a city treatment plant (invented data for practice). BOD (biochemical oxygen demand) is the oxygen microbes would use to break down the organic matter.

sewage-treatment-s2.title: Dissolved oxygen in a river below a sewage outfall, before and after a plant upgrade

plot.label: Line graph of dissolved oxygen in milligrams per liter at distances from 0 to 40 kilometers below a sewage outfall: before the upgrade it drops from 8.5 to a low of 3 at 10 km and recovers to 8 at 40 km; after the upgrade it dips only to 7.5 at 10 km; invented data

items.q: What percent of the BOD in raw sewage is removed by the end of secondary treatment?

mistakes.why: That is the share left (20 of 220). The share removed is (220 - 20) / 220 × 100.
That is the share removed by primary treatment alone (220 to 150). The question asks through secondary.

items.q: Which stage removes the most BOD?
options: Primary treatment, from 220 to 150 mg/L
Secondary, from 150 to 20 mg/L
Tertiary treatment, from 20 to 5 mg/L
Each stage removes the same amount

why.correct: Secondary treatment lowers BOD from 150 to 20 mg/L, a drop of 130. Primary removes 70, tertiary 15.
options: That is a drop of 70 mg/L, less than secondary.
Right: a drop of 130 mg/L.
That is a drop of 15 mg/L.
The drops are 70, 130 and 15 mg/L.

items.q: Why does secondary treatment remove so much BOD?
options: Microbes in aerated tanks eat it
Screens catch the large objects in the sewage
Chlorine dissolves the organic matter
Settling tanks let the dissolved matter sink

why.correct: In secondary treatment, aerated tanks let bacteria and other microbes eat the dissolved organic matter, so it is broken down in the plant instead of in the river.
options: Right: the plant uses oxygen so the river does not have to.
Screens act at the start and remove little BOD.
Chlorine kills germs; it is not the main BOD step.
Settling is primary treatment; dissolved organics do not sink.

items.q: Phosphorus falls from 4.5 to 0.5 mg/L only after tertiary treatment. Why does that step matter for the lake downstream?
options: It raises the water temperature for fish
It adds oxygen directly to the lake
It kills the bacteria in the sewage
It keeps out a nutrient algae need

why.correct: Primary and secondary treatment leave most phosphorus. Removing it in tertiary treatment keeps the limiting nutrient out of the lake, which prevents algal blooms and the oxygen drop that follows.
options: Phosphorus removal does not change temperature.
Removing phosphorus prevents the oxygen drop; it does not add oxygen.
Disinfection kills bacteria; phosphorus removal targets a nutrient.
Right: less phosphorus, less eutrophication.

items.q: Before the upgrade, where in the river was dissolved oxygen lowest?
options: Right at the outfall, at 8.5 mg per L
40 km below the outfall, at 8.0 mg per L
About 10 km below, at 3.0 mg per L
5 km below the outfall, at 5.0 mg per L

why.correct: Before the upgrade DO fell to 3.0 mg per L about 10 km below the outfall, then recovered downstream.
options: DO is still high at the outfall; it falls downstream.
By 40 km the river has nearly recovered.
Right: the low point of the solid line.
DO falls further, to 3.0, at 10 km.

items.q: Why was dissolved oxygen lowest some distance downstream rather than right at the outfall?
options: Sewage warms up as it flows and boils off oxygen
Microbes use oxygen as the waste flows
Fish gather 10 km downstream and use the oxygen
The river gets deeper at 10 km

why.correct: Microbes in the river break down the organic matter as the water flows. Their oxygen use takes time to pull DO down, so the low point is downstream; then the river recovers as the organic matter is used up and oxygen mixes back in.
options: Flowing water does not heat enough to explain this.
Right: decomposition takes time and distance.
Fish use little oxygen compared with decomposers.
Depth is not shown and does not explain the curve.

items.q: At 10 km below the outfall, find the percent change in dissolved oxygen from before to after the upgrade.

mistakes.why: You divided by the after value. Divide by the before value, 3.0 mg per L.
250% is 7.5 as a percent of 3.0. Subtract first: (7.5 - 3.0) / 3.0 × 100.

items.q: Which claim is best supported by the two curves?
options: The upgrade removed most waste
The upgrade added oxygen to the river at 40 km
The river was healthier before the upgrade
The upgrade moved the low point farther downstream

why.correct: After the upgrade the oxygen dip almost disappears, so better treatment removed most of the oxygen-demanding waste before it reached the river.
options: Right: the dip shrank from 3.0 to 7.5 mg per L at its low point.
Both curves are near 8 to 8.5 mg per L at 40 km.
DO was much lower before the upgrade.
The low point stays near 10 km; it just became much smaller.

items.q: Put the stages of a sewage treatment plant in order.
options: Screens and grit chambers remove large objects and sand
Primary settling tanks let solids sink as sludge
Aerated tanks let microbes break down dissolved organic matter
Tertiary filters and chemicals remove nitrogen and phosphorus
Chlorine or UV light kills remaining germs
Clean water is released to a river or lake

why.correct: Physical removal, then biological breakdown, then nutrient removal, then disinfection, then discharge.

items.q: What happens in primary sewage treatment?
options: Microbes break down dissolved organic matter
Chemicals remove nitrogen and phosphorus
Ultraviolet light kills the bacteria
Solids settle out of the water in tanks

why.correct: Primary treatment is physical: screens remove large debris, and wastewater sits in settling tanks so solids sink as sludge and grease floats off.
options: That is secondary treatment.
That is tertiary treatment.
That is disinfection, the last step.
Right: a physical process using gravity.

items.q: What is done with the sludge removed during treatment?
options: It is released straight into the river
It is added to the drinking water supply
It is digested, dried and disposed of
It is shipped to the ocean and dumped

why.correct: Sludge is digested by microbes (often making methane that can be burned for energy), then dried and landfilled, incinerated, or, if clean enough, used as fertilizer.
options: That would undo the treatment.
Sludge is waste, not drinking water.
Right: and digestion can yield methane for energy.
Ocean dumping of sludge is banned in the United States.

items.q: How does a household septic system treat wastewater?
options: Chlorine tablets in the toilet clean the water
Solids settle; soil filters the liquid
The water is piped to a city treatment plant
The wastewater evaporates from an open pond

why.correct: Wastewater flows into an underground tank where solids settle and bacteria break some down; the liquid flows out into a drain field, where soil filters it and microbes break down what is left.
options: Septic systems rely on settling and soil, not chlorine tablets.
Right: a small, two-part system for one home.
That describes a sewer system, not a septic system.
A septic tank is buried and sealed.

items.q: In some older cities, storm drains and sewers share one pipe. What problem does this cause during heavy rain?
options: Raw sewage overflows into rivers
The extra water makes the treatment work better
Rainwater freezes in the pipes and blocks them
Sludge turns into drinking water

why.correct: Heavy rain overwhelms the combined system, so untreated sewage mixed with stormwater overflows into rivers (a combined sewer overflow), adding germs and oxygen-demanding waste.
options: Right: a combined sewer overflow.
The plant is overwhelmed, not helped.
Freezing is not the problem described.
That is not what happens.

items.q: A city of 80,000 people produces about 300 liters of wastewater per person per day. Write the setup for the liters the plant treats per day, then give the answer in millions of liters.

why.correct: $80{,}000\,\text{people} \times \frac{300\,\text{L}}{\text{person}} = 24{,}000{,}000\,\text{L}$ a day, which is 24 million liters or $2.4 \times 10^{7}$ L.

mistakes.why: Multiply people by liters per person so the people cancel.
You divided. Multiply people by liters per person: 24,000,000 L.

items.q: A town's treatment plant has primary and secondary treatment only, and the lake below it has summer algal blooms. Justify adding tertiary treatment.

why.correct: The justification names what tertiary treatment removes (phosphorus and nitrogen) and how that helps (no nutrient supply for blooms, so no oxygen crash).

specific.frame: Tertiary treatment removes ___, which reduces algal blooms because ___.

removes.label: What it removes
options: phosphorus and nitrogen
large objects such as rags and sticks
heat from the water

why.1: Screens remove large objects at the start of treatment.
why.2: Treatment does not remove heat; that is about thermal pollution.

because.label: How it helps
options: algae no longer get the limiting nutrients they need to bloom
the water becomes too cold for algae
chlorine kills all the algae in the lake

why.1: Tertiary treatment does not cool the water.
why.2: Chlorine is used at the plant, not added to the lake.

specific.model: Tertiary treatment removes phosphorus and nitrogen, which reduces algal blooms because algae no longer get the limiting nutrients they need to bloom, so the lake avoids the oxygen drop when blooms die.
